title: Pricing by hours per project for Locksmith and door installation
audience: Locksmith and door installation owners who price short attendances and installs from estimated hours, and need a cost per productive hour they can defend.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures, including van and stock costs
Estimate an attendance or an install in named lines, including travel and checking time
Build a quote from hours, a buffer and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why short attendances need hours
instruction.body: A locksmith attendance is short, often at unsocial hours, and it carries travel time that does not shrink with the size of the job. A lockout that opens in 20 minutes can still take 45 minutes once travel and assessment are counted. Hours make that visible. Record the time for every attendance from the first job, because the figure is what makes an after-hours surcharge defensible.

instruction.heading: Work out the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Divide the year's total running costs by the chargeable hours. Running costs include wages with on-costs where you employ anyone, the van, tools, stock held, insurance, state licence fees, phone, dispatch software and administration. Use chargeable hours, not paid hours. Business.gov.au says on-costs such as leave and superannuation belong in the hourly figure. The vendor listings found for Victoria give job prices but no hourly rate for locksmiths, so the rate must come from the owner's own figures.

instruction.heading: Estimate the attendance in named lines
instruction.body: Name each line: travel to the site, assessment, the opening or rekey work, stock and parts, set-up and checking time, and any after-hours time billed separately. Waiting on a call-out is also a cost and should be recorded. A checklist of common jobs, such as a rekey, a lockout or a lock replacement, lets you build standard times from your own records.

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the chargeable hours by the cost per productive hour to get the cost of the job. Add a buffer for unexpected work, such as a lock type you did not expect. Xero's Australian guide suggests 10 to 20 per cent for unexpected work. Then set the price with a margin: the price is cost divided by one minus the margin. Add stock and parts at cost plus a stated markup if your policy allows, and apply your minimum charge and after-hours line.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest and review the estimates
instruction.body: State the attendance basis, the after-hours terms, the parts, what the client must provide, such as access and authority to change the lock, and how long the quote is valid. Record actual attendance time for at least the first ten jobs of each type and compare it with the estimate. If the variance stays above your threshold, change the standard time or the buffer.

procedure: Gather the year's total business costs and the chargeable hours from the same period.
Divide total costs by chargeable hours to get the cost per productive hour, and date the figure.
Name each line of the attendance or install and estimate its time as a range.
Add travel, assessment and checking time as named lines.
Add a buffer for unexpected work, then multiply the total hours by the cost per productive hour.
Apply the margin, then the stock policy, the after-hours line and the minimum charge.
Write the quote with scope, hours basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
Record actual attendance time after each job and compare it with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A locksmith is asked to rekey a residential cylinder during business hours. The estimate is 1 hour on site, 0.5 hours of travel and 0.25 hours of set-up and checking, a total of 1.75 hours. The owner's cost per productive hour is $85 (illustrative). The buffer is 10 per cent (illustrative). The target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the cost, what is the price, and how does the price compare with the vendor ranges?
workedExamples.reasoning: With a 10 per cent buffer the time is 1.925 hours. At $85 an hour the cost is $163.63 (illustrative). A 25 per cent margin on price gives a price of $163.63 divided by 0.75, which is $218.17 (illustrative). The Quote Yard's Victorian vendor ranges are a business-hours callout of $95 to $190 and a cylinder rekey of $48 to $130 (vendor estimates, 26 September 2026). If both lines are needed, the vendor's ranges add to $143 to $320. The illustrative $218 sits inside that band. It sits above the callout range on its own, so the owner should show the customer that the price includes the rekey and the time, and confirm that the cost, not the vendor band, supports it.

equipmentAndPpe: Time log for each attendance, with estimated and actual columns
Stock record for cylinders and parts used

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, van, tools, stock, insurance, licence fees and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out travel and assessment time on a short attendance
commonErrors.prevention: Add these as named lines on every quote, even when the attendance is short.

commonErrors.error: Quoting with no exclusions or client inputs
commonErrors.prevention: List what is excluded, what the client provides, and the access and authority assumptions.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Pricing guidance only. The ACCC says misleading statements about prices are prohibited, and state fair trading rules differ. Check the rules for your state.
Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. This lesson does not state those rates.

Licensing: Victoria's locksmith licence position is unresolved in the research, so check it with the regulator before you use any Victorian cost or price in a quote. New South Wales and Queensland both require a locksmith licence. Check the licence class and fees for each state where you work, and include them in the cost per productive hour.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows scope, hours basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the owner's own records and dated.
Actual attendance time is recorded for at least the first ten jobs of each type and compared with the estimate.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Quote showing scope, hours basis, exclusions and validity
Attendance time log with estimated and actual hours
summary: Start every attendance quote from named hours.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, not paid time.
Travel, assessment and checking time are named lines, not hidden extras.
Compare estimates with actual time, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour for a locksmith?
options: Only the wage of the lowest-paid worker
The price the client pays, plus any deposit taken
Wages with on-costs, van, tools, stock, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours
The average call-out price that competitors advertise

knowledgeChecks.question: An attendance estimated at 1.5 hours takes 3 hours. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual time, find the cause, and change the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate alone, since the customer has already paid
Cut paid hours for the crew on the next job
Raise the price for this customer's next job only

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a quote need an exclusions list?
options: To keep the margin secret from the customer
To show what the price covers, so scope changes can be priced and disputes reduced
To make the quote longer for the customer to read
To lower the customer's expectations of the work
